pass_a_gloss: [continued quotation] from you a sign to see. Counting worth very little (ὀλίγου ... ἀξιοῦντες λόγου) the voices of the saints, through which it was likely they could learn that he was the Christ, they sought God-signs (θεοσημίας); whence the Savior said to those sent by John 'Going, report to John what you hear and see: blind see again, lame walk' etc. And the Greeks seeking brilliance (λαμπρότητα) in diction and words, consider foolishness the manner (τρόπον) of the dispensation with flesh (τῆς μετὰ σαρκὸς οἰκονομίας), and say: Why at all was it needed that the Word from God, being God by nature, able by will (θελήσει) and nod (νεύματι) to accomplish what he purposes, become man and endure death? how could a virgin (παρθένον) bear? how will rise what was corrupted (κατεφθαρμένον) by death? But nothing unlikely (ἀπεικός) that they say such: 'For the natural (ψυχικός) man does not receive the things of the Spirit; for it is foolishness to him'; but to us it is power (δύναμις) and wisdom (σοφία) of God; for God and Father saved through him the [world] under heaven, as through the power being in him naturally (φυσικῶς) and the ineffable wisdom, clearly his own (ἑαυτοῦ); for wisdom and power of God and Father is the Son, through which all things were brought (παρῆκται) to coming-to-be (γένεσιν), and being made are preserved (σώζεται). And if anyone, he says, should choose to compare (ἀντεξετάσαι) the [power] in God with the powers of men, he will surely observe (καταθρήσει) that what seems of divine works to have been done as in weakness (ἀσθενείᾳ) perhaps, and as not with whole power of the maker, is beyond and better than all human strength (ἰσχύος); in this same way you will think also of wisdom, that what seems foolish is wiser than men. As if to the magnitudes and beauties of the elements (στοιχείων), heaven I mean and sun and other stars and fire and water and the rest, one wished to compare the small and least of creatures (κτισμάτων), very little will be found in these power and wisdom, and as from being inferior (ἡττῆσθαι) ... one might seem to be; but none of those among us could become, not even of such ... a maker (ἐργάτης). Truly then, that the weak of God is stronger than men, and the foolish of God wiser than men. So the dispensation (οἰκονομία) has the all-wise (πάνσοφον), for Christ has reigned (βεβασίλευκε) understandingly (συνετῶς) over all under heaven in wisdom. [Lemma 1 Cor 2:1] Proclaiming to you the testimony (μαρτύριον) of God. Testimony of God he calls Christ; for God and Father testified about him saying 'This is my Son the beloved in whom I was well pleased.' [Lemma 1 Cor 2:3] And I in weakness and in fear etc. For though using so moderate (μετρίᾳ) instruction (ὑφηγήσει), I feared greatly, he says, lest being found better than the understanding (διανοίας) in us [you], they might benefit nothing but rather harm; for to infants (νηπίοις) in mind a tender (τρυφερός) and gentle (εὐαφής) word fits for knowing, 'but solid food (στερεὰ τροφή) is of the perfect (τελείων), those having through habit (ἕξιν) the senses (αἰσθητήρια) trained for discernment of good and evil.' So, he says, the word to you came as in much weakness, and not in whole power of the initiator (μυσταγωγοῦ); nor in persuasions (πειθοῖς) of human wisdom but in demonstration (ἀποδείξει) of spirit and power, that your faith be not in wisdom of men but in power of God; for to the preaching the apostles added also God-signs, making the matter a clear demonstration of needing to believe that God in these through the Spirit and through the deeds themselves has been attested (μεμαρτύρηται); as using an ineffable (ἀῤῥήτῳ) and inexpressible (ἀφράστῳ) power and working, and accomplishing easily the wonder-works (τερατουργίας). For the little myths (μυθάρια) of Greeks would fittingly need the word fighting alongside (συνασπίζοντος) and as it were wrapping up (περιστέλλοντος) the unloveliness (ἀκαλλές) in them; but sufficient to the divine preaching is a bare (ψιλός) and gentle word, attested as in power of God.
pass_b_english: […] “to see a sign from you” (Matthew 12:38). So, counting the words of the saints as worth almost nothing, words through which they could well have learned that he was the Christ, they kept demanding signs from God. That is why the Savior said to those sent by John, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk,” and so on (Matthew 11:4–5).

The Greeks, for their part, seek brilliance of diction and argument, and they think even the way of the dispensation in the flesh to be foolishness. They say, “Why was it necessary at all for the Word who is from God, being God by nature and able to accomplish whatever he purposes by will and nod, to become man and to endure death? How could a virgin give birth?” they say. “And how will what death has destroyed rise again?” But it is not at all surprising that they say such things: “For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

But to us it is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). For through him God the Father has saved the whole world under heaven, as through the power that is naturally his and through his own ineffable wisdom. For the Son is the wisdom and power of God the Father, through whom all things were brought into being and, once made, are preserved.

And if anyone, he says, should choose to measure the power that is in God against the powers of men, he will certainly see that whatever among the divine works may seem to have been done as in weakness, and as it were not with the full power of its Maker, is beyond and better than all human strength. You will understand wisdom in exactly the same way: what seems to be foolish is wiser than men. Suppose someone wished to compare the small and least of created things with the size and beauty of the elements, I mean heaven and the sun and the other stars, and fire and water and the rest. The power and wisdom found in the small things would be very slight, and, judged by their inferiority at least, it might seem a [lacuna] sort of thing. Yet no one among us could become the maker even of things so [lacuna]. Truly, then, “the weakness of God is stronger than men, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25). So the dispensation holds all wisdom, for Christ has reigned with understanding, in wisdom, over the whole world under heaven.

“Proclaiming to you the testimony of God” (1 Corinthians 2:1). He calls Christ the testimony of God, for God the Father bore witness to him, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

“And I was with you in weakness and in fear,” and so on (1 Corinthians 2:3). Although I used such modest instruction, he says, I was very much afraid that my words, if they proved too lofty for the understanding you had, would do you no good but rather harm. For those who are infants in mind, a tender and gentle word would suit their learning, “but solid food is for the mature, for those who by practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). So my word to you, he says, came as in great weakness, and not with the full power of one who teaches the mysteries. Nor was it “in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

For to their preaching the apostles added signs from God as well. They made the deed itself a clear demonstration that one must believe that God was attested in them, through the Spirit and through the deeds themselves, since they used a certain ineffable and inexpressible power and working and performed their wonders with ease. The little myths of the Greeks would naturally need an eloquence to fight in their defense and, as it were, to cover up their ugliness. But for the divine preaching a plain and gentle word suffices, attested as it is by the power of God.

choices.why: Divine signs or wonders, as the Jews sought.
Read as ὑμῖν, a common itacism; the sense requires the Corinthians' understanding.

notes: Pass A gloss written from the Greek of this row; Pass B checked clause by clause against it (negation, agency, modality, doctrine).
Scripture citations placed beside the clause, full book name and chapter:verse; LXX Psalm numbers converted.

τῆς ἑαυτοῦ δηλονότι rendered as plain English instead of the stiff tag 'his own, that is'; lacunae moved to where the print has them: the gap stands before τις (the subject is the power and wisdom found in small things, not 'one'), and the second gap falls after οὕτως ('things so [lacuna]'), before ἐργάτης; title uses lowercase 'than' like the book's other titles. Second review: doctrine/agency: 'the power that is in him by nature', right after 'through him' (the Son), let readers take 'him' as the Son; τῆς ἐνούσης αὐτῷ φυσικῶς and τῆς ἑαυτοῦ refer to the Father, whose natural power and own wisdom the Son is (Cyril's point in the next sentence), so now 'the power that is naturally his and ... his own ineffable wisdom' with the Father as subject; 'the power of God and wisdom' reordered to 'the power and wisdom of God' (stiff order); ἐν πειθοῖς σοφίας ἀνθρωπίνης 'in the persuasions' was a calque, now 'in persuasive words of human wisdom'.
